<reason>A genuinely contested, high-quality debate. A built a coherent case (gatekeeping, distorted research agendas, erosion of languages' scientific function) and a sharp late distinction between English as widest channel and English as required passport, plus a fair hit that the motion judges the actual balance, not a repaired arrangement. But B controlled the decision frame from B2.1 onward: A's own remedy keeps English dominant in science and business, so the harms look policy-transmitted and fixable while the connectivity goods look structural. B's pressure questions extracted a real concession (A could not name one knowledge system destroyed specifically by English) and B redeployed it through the close. B also answered A's translation-dispersal point with the stronger developed mechanism (stock vs. flow, pivot structure, hub vs. N² links), which A never re-answered. A's rebuttals were honest and substantive but mostly defensive, re-establishing its own distinction rather than damaging B's goods. B made the debate easier to decide: fixable costs against structural gains, with the cause preserved by A's own solution.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1's catch that A's remedy preserves English dominance, converted into Q1 and compounded by Q2, which forced A4.3's admission that no knowledge system could be tied specifically to English dominance; B then cited that concession in both later speeches. Runner-up: B4.2's stock-vs-flow answer on machine translation, showing fragmentation would hurt the smallest languages hardest.</best_rebuttal>
